outcomes: Compare OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Haystack, PydanticAI and Semantic Kernel by workload fit and control model.
Distinguish framework abstractions from underlying agent architecture and application-owned safety controls.
Build one framework-neutral task contract and benchmark adapter behavior consistently.
Select a framework using task success, tool safety, grounding, traceability, latency, maintainability and ecosystem constraints.
Explain lock-in, deployment, observability and migration trade-offs.
prerequisites: Stage 6 Topics 1–7: agent loops, patterns, graph orchestration and HITL
Python typing, tool schemas, API integration and test design

glossary.definition: A library that packages abstractions for model calls, tools, state, orchestration, evaluation or observability.
A boundary that maps one framework's API into a stable application-owned task contract.
A typed request/result interface that allows multiple frameworks to solve the same task.
A repeatable runner that measures quality, safety, grounding, latency and cost against fixed cases.
The effort required to move prompts, tools, state, traces and orchestration to another implementation.
Application-owned policy for identity, authorization, budgets, approval, tenancy and side effects.

explanation.problem: Choosing an agent framework from a tutorial or popularity ranking is risky. Frameworks optimize for different abstractions: handoffs and tool calls, role-based teams, data and retrieval workflows, typed Python contracts, component pipelines or enterprise plugin ecosystems. A framework can accelerate implementation while still leaving authorization, tenant isolation, durable side effects and quality evaluation to your application.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Think of frameworks as different toolkits for building the same class of system. OpenAI Agents SDK is oriented around agents, tools, handoffs, guardrails and tracing in the OpenAI ecosystem. It is a natural candidate when you want a direct agent-and-tool programming model and its supported runtime integrations.

CrewAI emphasizes role-oriented agents, tasks, crews and flows. It can be a useful fit when a workflow is naturally expressed as a team of specialist roles coordinated toward a shared objective. The role metaphor is not a substitute for authorization: each worker still needs an explicit tool allow-list and budget.

LlamaIndex is strongly associated with data-centric LLM applications: connectors, indexing, retrieval, query engines and agents that use data tools. It is worth evaluating when enterprise knowledge, document ingestion and retrieval are central to the workload.

Haystack provides composable components and pipelines for search, RAG and agentic applications. It is a candidate when explicit component graphs, retrieval pipelines and modular backend composition are important.

PydanticAI emphasizes typed inputs, dependencies and validated structured outputs in Python. It is attractive when correctness at application boundaries, dependency injection and testable typed contracts are priorities.

Microsoft Semantic Kernel provides a plugin/function-oriented SDK and orchestration capabilities across supported language ecosystems. It is worth evaluating in organizations already invested in Microsoft and .NET/enterprise integration patterns. Check the exact language and orchestration feature maturity in the version you intend to deploy.

Do not compare frameworks by writing six unrelated demos. Define one task contract, one dataset, identical tool permissions and one evaluation harness. Run the same task through each adapter. Measure task completion, tool correctness, tenant isolation, citations, approval behavior, p50/p95 latency, token/cost usage, trace quality and developer effort. Record framework version, model, prompt, tool schema and configuration so the comparison is reproducible.

Keep a framework-neutral application boundary. Your domain layer owns identity, tenant scope, authorization, business rules, idempotency, HITL and audit. The framework adapter translates model/tool orchestration into your typed contract. This makes it possible to swap orchestration libraries without rewriting domain logic. Avoid storing business-critical state only in framework-specific memory or hidden runtime objects.

A framework choice is contextual, not a permanent identity. Start with the smallest abstraction that meets requirements. If a simple deterministic workflow is enough, do not introduce an agent framework. If retrieval dominates, evaluate data-centric libraries. If graph state and resumability dominate, evaluate graph orchestration. If typed Python interfaces dominate, evaluate typed-agent libraries. Validate current APIs, licensing, security posture, release cadence and supported deployment model before adoption.
explanation.mentalModel: Define one task contract → build a neutral adapter → implement candidate frameworks → run identical evaluations → compare trade-offs → choose the simplest fit.
limitations: Framework APIs and feature maturity change; pin versions and re-check official documentation before adoption.
Benchmarks can be biased by prompts, model choice, retrieval quality, caching and infrastructure.
A framework's guardrail feature does not replace application authorization or tenant isolation.
Tracing may contain sensitive prompts, tool arguments and retrieved documents; apply redaction and retention controls.
A rich framework may increase dependency weight, cold start time and operational complexity.
Framework-neutral adapters reduce lock-in but cannot erase framework-specific state and workflow semantics.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: Choosing an agent framework is like choosing a backend web framework. They can all serve an API, but their routing, dependency injection, middleware, ecosystem and deployment trade-offs differ. You compare them using the same requirements and tests, not by counting features on a landing page.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: Use a weighted score from 0 to 5. Example weights: task success 25%, tool safety 25%, grounding 20%, traceability 15%, latency 10%, maintainability 5%. If a candidate scores [4,5,4,4,3,4], weighted score is 0.25×4 + 0.25×5 + 0.20×4 + 0.15×4 + 0.10×3 + 0.05×4 = 4.15/5. A high aggregate must not hide a safety failure: treat critical safety criteria as hard gates, not compensable points.
explanation.productionImpact: Production selection requires pinned dependencies, compatibility tests, security review, trace redaction, reproducible evals, per-tenant budgets, explicit control-plane ownership, deployment footprint measurement, upgrade policy and a migration plan for prompts, state and traces.

useCase.scenario: Compare six candidate frameworks on one ecommerce support/refund task. Each adapter receives the same tenant-scoped request and registered tools, returns a typed result, citations and trace, and must require human approval for a high-value refund.
inputs: Identical tool schemas and tenant policy
Evaluation weights and hard safety gates
constraints: All candidates use the same task, data and permission set.
Tool authorization and tenant checks remain application-owned.
High-value refund requires HITL regardless of framework.
A candidate failing a hard safety gate cannot win on aggregate score.
Record framework/model versions and runtime configuration.
outputs: Decision record with rationale and migration risk
useCase.successMetric: Select a framework that passes every hard safety gate and achieves the best measured workload fit with acceptable operational cost.

trustBoundaries: Framework-generated tool calls are proposals; domain gateway authorizes every call.
Tenant identity comes from authenticated application context, not model output.
Framework memory and traces are treated as potentially sensitive data.
Approval decisions are handled by application-owned HITL controls.
Benchmark outputs are not trusted until citations, tool calls and policy gates are validated.
failurePaths: Unequal test inputs: invalidate the comparison and rerun identical fixtures.
Framework bypasses domain gateway: fail hard safety gate.
Missing citations: score grounding as failed even if prose looks plausible.
Trace leakage: redact sensitive fields and stop unsafe trace export.
Unpinned versions: mark result non-reproducible and pin dependencies.
Framework-specific state lock-in: document export and migration strategy.

workedExample.problem: Evaluate a candidate framework on a high-value refund support task without allowing framework-specific code to bypass domain policy.
workedExample.input: tenant=tenant-a; order=ORD-7; intent=refund; amount=₹12,500; allowed tools=order_lookup, policy_search, refund_quote.

steps.reasoning: Convert the task into a shared typed request and pass the same fixture to every candidate.
Candidate framework orchestrates three registered read/quote tools and returns answer, citations and trace.
Refund amount crosses ₹10,000; framework output must require a human decision before execution.
Apply weights to task success, tool safety, grounding, traceability, latency and maintainability after hard gates pass.
Compare score, ecosystem fit, operational footprint and migration risk; record why the winner fits this workload.

workedExample.expectedOutput: A reproducible comparison record. Any candidate that bypasses tenant policy or HITL fails regardless of its weighted score.

implementations.expectedResult: A shared adapter contract, deterministic reference implementation, tool allow-list, tenant validation, approval gate and normalized benchmark result.

failures.name: Feature checklist selection
failures.symptom: Team chooses the framework with the most demos and later struggles with deployment or maintenance.
failures.rootCause: No workload-specific benchmark or operational constraints.
failures.recovery: Define a weighted evaluation with hard safety gates and run representative tasks.
failures.regressionTest: Require decision record with task results, runtime and migration notes.

failures.name: Unequal comparison
failures.symptom: One framework uses a stronger model or better retrieval corpus and appears superior.
failures.rootCause: Candidates did not receive identical inputs, tools, prompts or model configuration.
failures.recovery: Pin shared model, dataset, tool schemas, policy and evaluation cases.
failures.regressionTest: Compare fixture and configuration hashes across all adapter runs.

failures.name: Framework bypasses authorization
failures.symptom: A tool call executes with a tenant ID or role invented by the model.
failures.rootCause: Framework tool registry is treated as the final security boundary.
failures.recovery: Route all tools through application-owned authorization and tenant context.
failures.regressionTest: Attempt cross-tenant tool call and assert zero domain side effects.

failures.name: Tracing leaks sensitive data
failures.symptom: Prompt, document or tool argument secrets appear in external trace storage.
failures.rootCause: Tracing enabled without data classification, redaction or retention policy.
failures.recovery: Redact before export, restrict access and apply retention controls.
failures.regressionTest: Inject a secret marker and assert it is absent from exported trace.

failures.name: Hidden state lock-in
failures.symptom: Migration requires rewriting workflow state and memory stored only in framework internals.
failures.rootCause: Domain state coupled to framework-specific object formats.
failures.recovery: Own durable domain state and define exportable checkpoint/trace contracts.
failures.regressionTest: Round-trip a persisted workflow through framework-neutral schema.

practice.guided: Map each framework to its strongest abstraction and name one workload where that abstraction is useful.
practice.independent: Implement two adapters against the shared contract and run identical fixtures. Compare tool safety, citations, latency, trace and developer effort.
practice.realWorld: Run a small pilot for a support/refund agent. Keep authentication, tenancy, approvals and side effects in a shared domain gateway while swapping framework adapters.
practice.expertExtension: Create a reproducible benchmark suite with pinned model/framework versions, p50/p95 latency, token/cost accounting, golden trajectories, adversarial tool calls, trace redaction and migration rehearsal.

steps: Load the fixed refund support fixture and shared tool contract.
Register two or more framework adapters behind the same interface.
Run identical cases with the same model, tool schemas and policy configuration.
Capture answer, citations, tool calls, trace, latency and token/cost data.

scenarioQuiz.question: What is the fairest way to compare two frameworks?
options: Use identical task fixtures, model, tools, policies and evaluation
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A controlled benchmark isolates framework behavior from differences in model, prompt, data and permissions.

scenarioQuiz.question: A framework offers built-in tool permissions. Who owns final tenant authorization?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Application-owned authorization remains the final boundary across frameworks and adapters.

scenarioQuiz.question: A candidate scores highest overall but allows a cross-tenant tool call. What is the decision?
options: Fail the hard safety gate and reject the candidate
Reduce the weight of tenant safety
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Critical safety properties are hard gates and cannot be compensated by latency or maintainability scores.

scenarioQuiz.question: What reduces framework lock-in most effectively?
options: Store all business state in framework memory
Use a shared typed contract and application-owned durable domain state
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A stable application boundary allows adapters to change without rewriting core domain policy and state.

rubric.evidence: Explain the six frameworks' core abstractions and choose by workload.
Two implementations normalize into one typed task/result interface.
Tool allow-list, tenant checks and HITL gates are enforced outside framework prompts.
Same fixtures/configuration and measured quality/runtime metrics.
Version pinning, trace redaction, deployment footprint and rollback strategy.

evidence: At least two candidate adapters run the same fixture.
Unsafe tool, tenant and approval cases fail closed.
Decision record includes framework versions and evidence.

codeWalkthrough.lines: class FrameworkAdapter(Protocol): def run(self, request, tools) -> AgentResult
codeWalkthrough.explanation: A stable adapter interface keeps application domain contracts independent from framework-specific orchestration APIs.

codeWalkthrough.lines: if call.name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS: raise PermissionError
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Framework tool registries are not the final security boundary; the application validates every proposed call.
Tenant context is derived from authenticated application state and checked for every domain operation.

codeWalkthrough.lines: if amount >= threshold and not approval_required: reject()
codeWalkthrough.explanation: High-impact policy remains consistent across frameworks and is enforced outside model instructions.
A safety failure cannot be offset by a better latency or maintainability score.
